newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan mulls economic impact of cool summer weather.
newsitem.headline: Japan mulls economic impact of cool summer weather.

text.p: Cooler-than-average temperatures across much of Japan for the July-September period, predicted on Thursday by Japan's Meteorological Agency, have drummed up talk about potential downward pressures on the economy.

The agency, in its latest three-month weather report, said temperatures would likely be cooler than usual in the heavily populated regions of eastern and western Japan -- which could have negative implications for businesses ranging from oil companies to beverage can producers.
The agency said also that Japan's rainy season was likely to stretch further into July, which analysts say normally throws a wet rag over consumer sentiment.

Japan's energy sector would likely take the biggest hit, as the country's blistering summers are normally a boon to both electricity producers and oil companies because of soaring air-conditioning use.

"A cooler summer would really be a double-whammmy for the oil companies, because they've already seen electric utilities buying less of their fuel oil in favour of natural gas and other fuel," said an oil industry analyst.
"The summer air-conditioning boom is something oil companies and utilities rely upon to pick up sales, so if it doesn't happen, they feel the pinch," he added.
"It's also worth noting that less demand for air conditioning in automobiles will reduce gasoline demand," he said.

A potential downturn in air-conditioning use, for which copper tubing is a primary component, was also a source of concern for some Japanese copper traders as well. Others were more sceptical of the report.
"If it really turns out to be a cool summer, demand from air-conditioner makers would fall. But the forecast is wrong pretty often," said one.
Japan aluminium traders also said a cooler summer could also cause them problems.
"A (cool summer) is a problem and would definitely have an impact. It dents demand for beverage cans and air conditioners," he said.
Another aluminium trader said the weather would make a difference of a few percent in Japan's annual aluminium demand of about 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes.
Akira Hiyoshi, an economist at Asahi Bank Ltd, felt that while Japan's longer-term economic rebound would not suffer because of the cooler weather, it could cause people to temporarily spend less.
"The recovery in private consumption will not be interrupted, but a cool summer will have a limited impact on dampening consumer sentiment somewhat," he said.
